# Overview

**Prerequisites:** Module 1 (cloud-native rasters, `terra`, bounding boxes from country polygons). Familiarity with `prioritizr` is helpful (see the reading tutorial).

::: {.callout-tip title="Peer programming"}
Work with a partner. Switch who codes occasionally and practice git commands and collaborative coding!
:::

The EU and Switzerland have both committed to protecting 30% of land by 2030. An optimizer can tell you which 30%, but only after you tell it what to protect *for*. In this module you will:

1.  Load three global layers and **clip them to Europe** (Switzerland included) (you write this part).
2.  Build four conservation plans, each protecting 30% of the land and maximising a different benefit: species richness, carbon, nature's contributions to people (NCP), or all three together.
3.  Ask who is inside each plan: **how many people** live in the protected land, and **which countries** are you solutions in.
4.  Optionally, explore **burden sharing** between countries, and take into account what is **already protected**.

## Setup

```{r}
#| label: setup
library(terra)
library(sf)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(rnaturalearth)
library(prioritizr)

dir.create("cache", showWarnings = FALSE)

# Remote reads should fail or retry rather than hang if the network stalls
setGDALconfig(c("GDAL_HTTP_TIMEOUT=60", "GDAL_HTTP_MAX_RETRY=3", "GDAL_HTTP_RETRY_DELAY=2"))
```

The layers:

| Layer | What it is | Where it lives |
|------------------------|------------------------|------------------------|
| `richness` | Combined IUCN species richness, 10 km, World Mollweide | local file in `data/` |
| `carbon` | Irrecoverable carbon (Noon et al. 2022) | cloud-optimised GeoTIFF, lon/lat |
| `ncp` | Number of nature's contributions to people a place ranks highly for, 0-19 (Chaplin-Kramer et al. 2019) | cloud-optimised GeoTIFF, lon/lat |

Population (GHS-POP 2020) is a fourth layer you pull yourself at the end. The last three layers are cloud-native files on [Source Cooperative](https://source.coop/cboettig): no account or key, just a lazy connection and a window read, like Module 1's satellite imagery.

# Load and clip to Europe

## 1. A polygon for Europe

We want Europe's countries, with Switzerland as one of them, not a hand-typed box. A few judgement calls are already made here: Russia is dropped (most of it is far outside the layers' useful window), and the crop removes territories such as Svalbard. We could also clip this to the EU.

```{r}
#| label: europe-polygon
# Planar geometry for the lon/lat crop below
sf_use_s2(FALSE)

europe <- ne_countries(scale = "medium", continent = "Europe", returnclass = "sf") |>
  filter(name != "Russia") |>
  st_make_valid() |>
  st_crop(xmin = -25, xmax = 45, ymin = 34, ymax = 72)

bbox <- st_bbox(europe)
bbox
```

## 2. Richness: crop a local raster

::: {.callout-note title="Your task"}
`data/Combined_SR_2025.tif` is global, in World Mollweide (metres). Crop it to Europe and call the result `richness`, with the layer named `richness`. Then plot it.

*Hint:* `europe` and `bbox` are in degrees. What happens if you crop a metres raster with degrees? Check `crs()` on both, and try it the naive way first so you see the failure.
:::

```{r}
#| label: richness-task
#| eval: false
richness_global <- rast("data/Combined_SR_2025.tif")

#next chunk
europe_proj <-    # europe -> transform to crs(richness_global) -> vect
richness <- crop(___, ___)
names(richness) <- "richness"
```

::: {.callout-note title="Solution" collapse="true"}
```{r}
#| label: richness-solution
richness_global <- rast("data/Combined_SR_2025.tif")

europe_proj <- europe |>
  st_transform(crs(richness_global)) |>
  vect()

richness <- crop(richness_global, europe_proj)
names(richness) <- "richness"
```
:::

```{r}
#| label: richness-plot
plot(richness, main = "Combined species richness")
```

"Richness" counts IUCN-assessed species whose *range map* overlaps each cell. Range maps are plausible extents, not confirmed presences, and 10 km is coarse next to real habitat.

## 3. Carbon: window-read a cloud-optimised GeoTIFF

::: {.callout-note title="Your task"}
The COG is at `https://s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/us-west-2.opendata.source.coop/cboettig/carbon/v2/cogs/irrecoverable_c_total_2024.tif` (put `/vsicurl/` in front of the URL to open it lazily). The same file is also served at `https://data.source.coop/cboettig/carbon/v2/cogs/irrecoverable_c_total_2024.tif`; if one address is slow or stalls, try the other. Open it, crop it to Europe's window, then get it onto the richness grid so the two stack.

*Hints:*

- The file is global at about 300 m, so a full-resolution read of Europe is hundreds of millions of pixels. A COG stores pre-computed coarser **overviews**: `rast(path, opts = "OVERVIEW_LEVEL=1")` opens a level that is 4 times coarser (try 0 to 4: how does speed change?).
- The COG is in lon/lat. `resample()` assumes two rasters already share a CRS and silently returns all `NA` when they don't, so use `project()`.
- `project()`'s `method` matters: your cells are much wider than the source pixels, so pick the method for *aggregating* (see `?project`), then plot it and look for speckled holes.
- Check `global(carbon, "max", na.rm = TRUE)` to confirm you didn't get an empty raster.
:::

```{r}
#| label: carbon-task
#| eval: false
carbon_cog <- rast("___", opts = "OVERVIEW_LEVEL=1")

carbon_window <- crop(___, ext(___))
carbon <- project(___, ___, method = ___)
names(carbon) <- "carbon"
```

::: {.callout-note title="Solution" collapse="true"}
```{r}
#| label: carbon-solution
# Source Cooperative serves the same file at two addresses; use whichever is faster for you
carbon_cog <- rast("/vsicurl/https://s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/us-west-2.opendata.source.coop/cboettig/carbon/v2/cogs/irrecoverable_c_total_2024.tif",
                   opts = "OVERVIEW_LEVEL=1")
# carbon_cog <- rast("/vsicurl/https://data.source.coop/cboettig/carbon/v2/cogs/irrecoverable_c_total_2024.tif",
#                    opts = "OVERVIEW_LEVEL=1")

carbon_window <- crop(carbon_cog, ext(bbox[c("xmin", "xmax", "ymin", "ymax")]))
carbon <- project(carbon_window, richness, method = "average")
names(carbon) <- "carbon"
plot(carbon)
```

The overview pixels are about 1 km and our cells are 10 km, so we are *aggregating*, not interpolating. `method = "bilinear"` reads only the four pixels nearest each cell centre, so a cell becomes `NA` if that one spot is a lake or a town. `"average"` uses every pixel in the cell and ignores `NA`s.
:::

```{r}

#carbon_cog <- rast("/vsicurl/https://s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/us-west-2.opendata.source.coop/cboettig/carbon/v2/cogs/irrecoverable_c_total_2024.tif",
 #                  opts = "OVERVIEW_LEVEL=1")
 carbon_cog_coop <- rast("/vsicurl/https://data.source.coop/cboettig/carbon/v2/cogs/irrecoverable_c_total_2024.tif",
                    opts = "OVERVIEW_LEVEL=1")

carbon_window_coop <- crop(carbon_cog, ext(bbox[c("xmin", "xmax", "ymin", "ymax")]))
carbon_coop <- project(carbon_window, richness, method = "average")
names(carbon_coop) <- "carbon"
plot(carbon_coop)
#results in exactly the same map, the data is the same just coming from different cloud hosts
```

## 4. NCP: the same recipe

NCP comes as a cloud-optimised GeoTIFF too, in the same Source Cooperative folder (`ncp/NCP_only_4326_cog.tif`, a score from 0 to 19 in lon/lat, about 2 km pixels). It is small enough that we do not need an overview. This is the carbon recipe again, so it is given: open lazily, crop, then `project()` onto the richness grid.

```{r}
#| label: ncp
ncp_cog <- rast("/vsicurl/https://s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/us-west-2.opendata.source.coop/cboettig/ncp/NCP_only_4326_cog.tif")
# ncp_cog <- rast("/vsicurl/https://data.source.coop/cboettig/ncp/NCP_only_4326_cog.tif")

ncp_window <- crop(ncp_cog, ext(bbox[c("xmin", "xmax", "ymin", "ymax")]))
ncp <- project(ncp_window, richness, method = "average")
names(ncp) <- "ncp"
plot(ncp)
```

::: {.callout-note title="Questions"}
1.  Why `"average"` again? What would `"sum"` do to a *score*, and why would that be wrong here (and right for something like a head count)?
2.  Where are the holes in the map? Check how many land cells are `NA` and which countries they are in. Is "no data" the same thing as "no NCP"?
3.  We are about to turn missing values into 0. What does that assume about NCP in those cells, and who could be affected?
:::

## 5. Stack, then clip to the *countries*

`crop()` takes a rectangle, so `grid` still holds sea, North Africa, and Turkey. A planner must not "protect" them. Two decisions:

- **Missing values on land:** treat missing carbon or NCP (lakes, glaciers, thin coverage) as 0 rather than dropping the cell.
- **Outside Europe's countries:** these cells must be `NA`, *not* 0, so the optimizer cannot select them.

::: {.callout-note title="Your task"}
Stack the three layers into one `grid` (starting from `richness`, so the chunk is safe to re-run), fill the missing values, then use `mask()` with the European polygon (`europe_proj`) to set everything outside to `NA`. Plot `grid` and count the cells that remain with `global(grid[["richness"]], "notNA")`.

*Think:* why mask *after* filling the zeros rather than before? And `mask()` has a `touches` argument: which setting do you want for a coastline?
:::

```{r}
#| label: assemble-task
#| eval: false
fill0 <- function(x) ifel(is.na(x), 0, x)

grid <- c(richness, ___, ___)
grid <- mask(grid, ___, touches = ___)
```

::: {.callout-note title="Solution" collapse="true"}
```{r}
#| label: assemble-solution
fill0 <- function(x) ifel(is.na(x), 0, x)

grid <- c(richness, fill0(carbon), fill0(ncp))
grid <- mask(grid, europe_proj, touches = FALSE)

writeRaster(grid, "cache/europe_grid.tif", overwrite = TRUE)

```

`touches = FALSE` keeps a cell only if its centre is inside a country, so sea cells that merely graze the coast are dropped.
:::

```{r}
#| label: layers-plot
plot(grid)
```

Each layer keeps its own units and legend.

::: {.callout-note title="Exercise"}
Before running anything: if you had to pick 30% of Europe, where would you protect? Write down a guess for each layer, then compare with the optimizer below.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Stuck or offline?"}
`grid <- rast("cache/europe_grid.tif")` loads a finished copy (you will also need `europe_proj` and `richness` from the richness step).
:::

# Four plans

There are no per-feature targets here. We fix a **budget** (protect 30% of the land) and ask `prioritizr` to pick the cells that give the **most benefit** for it. Every cell costs the same for now, so the budget is just 30% of the cells. "Benefit" is the sum of what the chosen cells hold, after each layer has been rescaled to run from 0 to 1.

::: {.callout-note title="Why rescale each layer to 0-1?"}
The objective *adds* the layers together, and the layers are in different units: richness averages about 247 species per cell, carbon about 14, NCP about 7. Added raw, richness would outweigh carbon roughly 17 to 1 before you have said anything about what matters. Rescaling each layer to 0-1 (its lowest cell becomes 0 and its highest becomes 1; `terra::stretch()` does this) puts them on one scale, so a weight of 2 means "twice as important" rather than "twice as important, times whatever the units happen to be".

Rescaling does not make the layers equal, and it is a choice, not a neutral step:

- It is set by the **extremes**. Carbon's highest cell is about 10 times its average, so most carbon cells end up close to 0 and carbon has less pull than its 0-1 scale suggests.
- It depends on the **study area**: add or drop a country and the minimum and maximum move, and so does the plan.
- Other choices exist (divide by the total, z-scores, ranks), and they give different plans. You can compare these if you are interested!
:::

## carbon alone

We set the problem up in `prioritizr` the way you would describe it in words: *choose the cells that hold the most carbon, without protecting more than 30% of the land.* In code that sentence has five parts, and each one is a line (or two) below:\

| Part | Question it answers | In the code below |
|------------------------|------------------------|------------------------|
| Planning units and cost | What can we choose from, and what does each cell cost? | `problem(uniform_cost, ...)`: every non-`NA` cell is a planning unit |
| Features | What do we want to protect? | `features = carbon_01` |
| Objective | What do we maximise, and under what budget? | `add_max_wtd_sum_objective(budget = budget_cells)` |
| Decisions | Is a cell all in or all out? | `add_binary_decisions()` |
| Solver | Which engine finds the answer? | `add_default_solver(...)` |

```{r}
#| label: plan-carbon
# PLANNING UNITS AND COST
# A raster with a 1 in every land cell and NA elsewhere. prioritizr treats each
# non-NA cell as a planning unit and its value as the cost of protecting it.
# Every cell costs the same for now, so "cost" just counts cells.
uniform_cost <- ifel(is.na(grid[["richness"]]), NA, 1)
names(uniform_cost) <- "cost"

# BUDGET
# 30% of the total cost = 30% of the land cells. This is the most we may protect.
budget_cells <- 0.3 * global(uniform_cost, "sum", na.rm = TRUE)[[1]]

# FEATURE
# What we want to protect: carbon, rescaled so the lowest cell is 0 and the
# highest is 1 (see the note above for why).
carbon_01 <- stretch(grid[["carbon"]], minv = 0, maxv = 1)

# THE PROBLEM (nothing is solved yet; this only describes it)
p_carbon <- problem(uniform_cost, features = carbon_01) |>      # cells to choose from + what to protect
  add_max_utility_objective(budget = budget_cells) |>   # maximise the summed feature value, within the budget
  add_binary_decisions() |>                             # each cell is protected (1) or not (0), never partly
  add_default_solver(gap = 0, verbose = FALSE)          # gap = 0: demand the exact best answer, not "within 10%"

# SOLVE
# force = TRUE: prioritizr flags single-feature problems as a likely mistake, and we want one here
sol_carbon <- solve(p_carbon, force = TRUE)

# The answer is a raster of 1s (protected) and 0s (not)
plot(sol_carbon, col = c("grey90", "darkgreen"), main = "Carbon alone, 30% of the land")
```

Two things to check. How many cells did it protect (`global(sol_carbon, "sum", na.rm = TRUE)`), and is that 30% of the land cells? Then look at the map: does it match where the carbon layer is high?

## richness and carbon

Same thing, with a second layer. With two layers and no weights, each counts equally.

```{r}
#| label: plan-richness-carbon
# A second feature, rescaled the same way
richness_01 <- stretch(grid[["richness"]], minv = 0, maxv = 1)

# Only the features change: two layers stacked with c(). Cost, budget, objective,
# decisions and solver are exactly as before.
p_richness_carbon <- problem(uniform_cost, features = c(richness_01, carbon_01)) |>
  add_max_wtd_sum_objective(budget = budget_cells) |>   # now maximises richness + carbon, each counting equally
  add_binary_decisions() |>
  add_default_solver(gap = 0, verbose = FALSE)

# No force = TRUE needed: there are two features now
sol_richness_carbon <- solve(p_richness_carbon)

plot(sol_richness_carbon, col = c("grey90", "darkgreen"), main = "Richness and carbon, 30% of the land")
```

::: {.callout-note title="Stop and think"}
Look back at the two chunks above. Which lines did you copy and paste, and which lines changed? Now imagine you also want NCP, a 10% budget, unequal weights, and a plan that locks in existing protected areas, and you want to compare a dozen of these.

1.  What are the things that vary between plans? Those are the arguments.
2.  What stays the same? That is the body.
3.  What would go wrong if you kept copying and pasting (and fixed a bug in only one copy)?

Sketch the function you would write before you read ours below.
:::

## Wrapping the steps in a function

One answer: the layers and weights are the arguments, the budget and cost have defaults, and the body is the code you just wrote.

```{r}
#| label: make-plan
# Weights say how much each layer counts; layers are rescaled to 0-1; the budget is a share of total cost.
make_problem <- function(richness = 0, carbon = 0, ncp = 0, population = 0,
                         budget = 0.3, cost = uniform_cost, locked_in = NULL) {
  weights <- c(richness = richness, carbon = carbon, ncp = ncp, population = population)
  weights <- weights[weights > 0]
  stopifnot("give at least one layer a weight above 0" = length(weights) > 0)

  features <- stretch(grid[[names(weights)]], minv = 0, maxv = 1)

  p <- problem(cost, features = features) |>
    add_max_wtd_sum_objective(budget = budget * global(cost, "sum", na.rm = TRUE)[[1]]) |>
    add_feature_weights(unname(weights)) |>
    add_binary_decisions() |>
    add_default_solver(gap = 0, verbose = FALSE)

  if (!is.null(locked_in)) p <- add_locked_in_constraints(p, locked_in)
  p
}

# force = TRUE, as before, so single-layer plans are allowed
make_plan <- function(...) solve(make_problem(...), force = TRUE)
```

Two functions rather than one: `make_problem()` builds the problem and `make_plan()` solves it. Why might it be useful to keep those separate? (Extension A hints at one reason.)

```{r}
#| label: plans
plans <- list(
  "1. richness"    = make_plan(richness = 1),
  "2. carbon"      = make_plan(carbon = 1),
  "3. NCP"         = make_plan(ncp = 1),
  "4. all three"   = make_plan(richness = 1, carbon = 1, ncp = 1)
)
```

Does the function reproduce the carbon plan you wrote by hand? This should be 0 (the number of cells that differ).

```{r}
#| label: check-function
global(abs(plans[["2. carbon"]] - sol_carbon), "sum", na.rm = TRUE)[[1]]
```

```{r}
#| label: plans-plot
switzerland <- europe |> filter(name == "Switzerland") |> st_transform(crs(grid))

plans |>
  lapply(\(s) as.data.frame(setNames(s, "protected"), xy = TRUE)) |>
  bind_rows(.id = "plan") |>
  ggplot() +
  geom_raster(aes(x, y, fill = factor(protected))) +
  geom_sf(data = switzerland, fill = NA, colour = "red") +
  facet_wrap(~plan) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("0" = "grey90", "1" = "darkgreen"), name = "protected") +
  coord_sf(crs = crs(grid)) +
  theme_void()
```

Switzerland is outlined in red. Compare Plans 1 to 3: where do they agree, and where do they pull apart?

## What does each plan hold?

Every plan uses exactly 30% of the land, so the interesting columns are the others: what share of each layer does a plan hold?

```{r}
#| label: summary-table
share_held <- function(sol, layer) {
  global(sol * grid[[layer]], "sum", na.rm = TRUE)[[1]] /
    global(grid[[layer]], "sum", na.rm = TRUE)[[1]]
}

summary_table <- lapply(plans, \(sol) {
  tibble::tibble(
    share_of_land = global(sol, "mean", na.rm = TRUE)[[1]],
    richness_held = share_held(sol, "richness"),
    carbon_held   = share_held(sol, "carbon"),
    ncp_held      = share_held(sol, "ncp")
  )
}) |> bind_rows(.id = "plan")

summary_table |> mutate(across(-plan, ~ round(.x, 2)))
```

# Your turn

::: {.callout-note title="Tasks"}
1.  Look at Plan 4, which gives every layer the same weight. Does it hold about the same share of richness, carbon and NCP? Why not? (*Hint:* compare how the three layers are distributed; the plots above are a start, and so is the note on rescaling.) Which layer is a 30% budget most and least efficient for?
2.  In Plan 4, change the weights (try `richness = 3`, then `ncp = 3`). Which layer moves the map most? Was that what you expected?
3.  Change `budget` to 0.1 and 0.5. Is the gain from protecting more land steady or does it flatten out?
4.  Swap `data/Amphibians_RWR_2025.tif` in as the richness layer (same grid, same crop and mask code). It upweights small-range species. How do Plans 1 and 4 change?
5.  Invent a planning group (a national park agency, the farmers' union, a tourism board). Choose its weights, write one sentence on why, run `make_plan()`, and add it to the table.
6.  Compare rescaling choices for the all-three plan: (a) raw values, (b) 0-1 as above, (c) each layer divided by its Europe-wide total. Build each version of `features` yourself, solve, and compare the share of each layer held and how many cells differ. Which layer wins under each? Which would you defend to a planning group, and why?
:::

# Exercise: how many people?

We left people out of the objective on purpose: we protected for nature first, and now we count who ends up inside. Population is the fourth layer.

Population (GHS-POP 2020, JRC) is a global COG at about 90 m: `population/raw/ghs-pop-2020-cog.tif` in the same Source Cooperative folder. It is 11.6 GB, so the lazy, windowed read matters even more than it did for carbon.

::: {.callout-note title="Your task"}
Read population for Europe, put it on `grid`, and work out how many people live inside the protected cells of each of the four plans.

*Hints:*

- It is the carbon recipe again: open lazily, crop, `project()` onto the richness grid. Use an overview (`OVERVIEW_LEVEL=3` is 16 times coarser, about 1.5 km) so you do not read all 90 m pixels.
- Population is a **count**, not a score. Which `method` adds people up as cells get bigger?
- **A trap:** each overview pixel holds the *average* of the pixels it covers, not their total. Summing overview pixels therefore undercounts people by the number of pixels averaged (here 16 x 16). Check your answer: the countries in `grid` hold about 570 million people.
- Keep population in **thousands** of people so the numbers stay readable.
- Missing population is 0 on land and `NA` outside, exactly as before. Re-use `fill0()` and `mask()`.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Solution" collapse="true"}
```{r}
#| label: population-solution
pop_cog <- rast("/vsicurl/https://s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/us-west-2.opendata.source.coop/cboettig/population/raw/ghs-pop-2020-cog.tif",
                opts = "OVERVIEW_LEVEL=3")
# pop_cog <- rast("/vsicurl/https://data.source.coop/cboettig/population/raw/ghs-pop-2020-cog.tif",
#                 opts = "OVERVIEW_LEVEL=3")
pop_window <- crop(pop_cog, ext(bbox[c("xmin", "xmax", "ymin", "ymax")]))

# Sum people into cells; overview pixels are averages of 16 x 16 pixels, so scale back up (and to thousands)
population <- project(pop_window, richness, method = "sum") * 16^2 / 1000
names(population) <- "population"

grid <- c(grid[[c("richness", "carbon", "ncp")]], mask(fill0(population), grid[["richness"]]))

# Total population on the grid, in millions (should be about 570)
global(grid[["population"]], "sum", na.rm = TRUE)[[1]] / 1000

# Millions of people inside each plan
sapply(plans, \(sol) global(sol * grid[["population"]], "sum", na.rm = TRUE)[[1]]) / 1000
```
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Questions"}
1.  Which plan has the most people inside it, and which the fewest? Population was never an objective, so is this a coincidence?
2.  What share of Europe's population is that, compared with the 30% of land? Who might welcome that, and who might object?
3.  Run `make_plan(richness = 1, carbon = 1, ncp = 1, population = 1)` (population as a fourth objective). How far does the map move, and what happens to the other three shares?
:::

# Exercise: which countries?

Conservation targets are national commitments, but the optimizer above only sees one big map. How much of each solution sits in each country?

::: {.callout-note title="Your task"}
Build a raster `country` on `grid` in which each cell holds the ID of the country it is in (`rasterize()` on the polygon, `field = "id"`), then write a function `country_burden(sol)` that returns, per country, the number of land cells, the number protected, and the **share of the country's land** that is protected.

Run it for Plan 4. Which countries carry the most protected land, in absolute terms and as a share of their own territory? Where is Switzerland?
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Solution" collapse="true"}
```{r}
#| label: country-solution
europe_proj$id <- seq_len(nrow(europe_proj))
country <- rasterize(europe_proj, grid, field = "id")

country_burden <- function(sol) {
  land <- zonal(uniform_cost, country, "sum", na.rm = TRUE)
  protected <- zonal(sol * uniform_cost, country, "sum", na.rm = TRUE)
  tibble::tibble(
    country   = europe_proj$name[land$id],
    cells     = land$cost,
    protected = protected[[2]],
    share     = protected[[2]] / land$cost
  )
}

country_burden(plans[["4. all three"]]) |>
  arrange(desc(share)) |>
  mutate(share = round(share, 2))
```
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Questions"}
1.  Plot the protected share by country for Plan 4. Is any country far above or below 30%? What is it about the layers that makes this happen?
2.  Do the four plans give the same ranking of countries? Which plan is most unequal?
3.  A cell is assigned by its centre. What does that do to small countries and to Switzerland's border?
:::

# Exercise: is the optimizer neutral?

::: {.callout-note title="Reflection"}
Write a short paragraph on where values entered even though you never told the solver to care about values: the layers, how they were rescaled, the 10 km grid, the 30% budget, the equal weights, treating missing cells as zero, using national borders as the unit of reporting, and who was left out of the polygon (Russia, microstates, overseas territories).
:::

# Optional extension A: burden sharing between countries

A single European plan is *efficient*: it picks the 30% that holds the most benefit. But as the country exercise shows, a few countries may carry most of the protected land while others protect almost none. Who should give up land, and how should that be decided?

::: {.callout-note title="Explore"}
Design and compare at least two alternatives to the pooled plan (for example, every country protects its own 30%, or every country protects at least a minimum share), and measure what each one costs in richness, carbon and NCP. `make_problem()` returns the problem before it is solved, and `?add_linear_constraints` is a place to start.

1.  Which countries gain or lose under your rule compared with the pooled plan? Where does Switzerland sit?
2.  What is the "price" of fairness here, in benefit held?
3.  "Equal share of land" is one idea of fairness. Others: equal share of cost, share proportional to wealth or to benefits received, or credit for what a country has already protected. Pick one and say how you would encode it and what data you would need.
:::

# Optional extension B: what is already protected?

Every plan above starts from a blank map. In reality much of Europe is already protected, which also changes the burden-sharing story: a country that already protects 25% has far less left to give than one with 5%.

::: {.callout-note title="Explore"}
The [World Database on Protected Areas (WDPA)](https://www.protectedplanet.net/) holds the boundaries of existing protected areas, and the `wdpar` package can download and clean them. Rasterise them onto `grid`, work out how much of each layer is already held, and re-run your plans with those cells **locked in** (see `?add_locked_in_constraints`).

1.  Which layer is least represented in existing protection? Which countries have already done most of their share?
2.  How different is the plan once you build on what exists?
3.  Is a cell protected on paper actually protected? What does WDPA not tell you?
:::

# Going further

- `add_boundary_penalties()` rewards connected plans. Run it on Plan 4 and compare the benefit held by a connected plan versus the scattered one, at the same budget. At 58,000 cells it will be slow, so try a coarser grid first (`aggregate(grid, 3)`).
- **Change the costs.** Real land is not uniformly priced. [EULOCC1K](https://doi.org/10.25829/xa7c12) (Spencer et al. 2025) gives European opportunity costs of conservation at 1 km, in €/ha/yr. Download the netCDF from the [EBV Data Portal](https://portal.geobon.org/ebv-detail?id=78&v=2), `project()` it onto `grid` (it is EPSG:3035), and pass it as `cost`; the budget is then 30% of total *cost* rather than 30% of cells. The Z-score version is built to equalise the burden between countries, which connects directly to Extension A. Is "cost" a different kind of variable from the benefits?

## When something fails

- **Carbon is all `NA`.** You used `resample()` instead of `project()`, or cropped the COG with a box in the wrong CRS.
- **Carbon is full of speckled holes.** Check the `method` in `project()`: you want to aggregate, not interpolate.
- **Richness crop returns one cell.** The box was in degrees and the raster is in metres.
- **`solve()` fails a presolve check.** Does at least one layer have a weight above 0? Is the budget big enough to hold any locked-in cells or country floors? Are there `NA` cells in the features that are not `NA` in the cost?
- **Network timeouts on the pulls.** Use `rast("cache/europe_grid.tif")`.
